title: Many customs
hook: veils, kneeling, silence or sung responses: customs differ from parish to parish
tomorrow: Two forms of the Latin rite

segments.voice: Yesterday, bells: the tower calling to Mass, the Angelus at noon, the slow toll for the dead. Your line was the bell calls. Which sound became your bell? Day one thousand four hundred three.

A lace veil, folded small, lives in the coat pocket of a woman who travels for work. On Sunday in one city, she puts it on, and so do several women around her. The next Sunday, in another city, she's the only one, and she wonders whether to take it off. In the first church the people kneel after the Lamb of God; in the second they stand until communion. One choir chants the responses in Latin. Across town, a guitar leads them in English. One parish keeps a long silence after communion. Another goes straight to the announcements. Same Mass. Same creed. Is somebody doing it wrong? Today, many customs.
screen: `A VEIL IN A COAT POCKET.` → `KNEEL HERE, STAND THERE.` → `IS SOMEBODY DOING IT WRONG?`

segments.voice: This question is old. Saint Augustine tells it in one of his letters. His mother, Monica, had moved to Milan, and she was troubled. Back home, she had fasted on Saturdays. In Milan the church didn't. Should she keep her old custom or take up the new one? Augustine went to the bishop of Milan, Ambrose, and asked. Ambrose's answer, as Augustine reports it: when I'm here, I don't fast on Saturday; when I'm in Rome, I do. Follow the custom of the church you're in. Augustine says he took that answer as if it had come from heaven. Paul had been there first. Writing to the Romans, who were arguing about food and holy days, he says in the Douay-Rheims: "One judgeth between day and day: and another judgeth every day: let every man abound in his own sense." Then he tells them to stop judging each other. The Church draws a line between what is shared and what is local. The faith, the sacraments, the heart of the Mass: these are one. The Second Vatican Council said the Church doesn't want a rigid sameness in matters that don't touch the faith or the good of the whole community. The instructions for Mass let the bishops of each country adapt postures, and they leave room for music, language and local devotion. So a veil worn by choice, a kneel or a stand, a chant or a hymn, can be different and both be faithful. Customs can still matter a great deal to the people who keep them. A grandmother's mantilla, a parish's long silence: these carry love. The question isn't whose custom wins. It's whether you can kneel beside someone else's.
screen: `MONICA'S QUESTION IN MILAN.` · `AMBROSE: FOLLOW THE CHURCH YOU'RE IN.` · `PAUL: LET EVERY MAN ABOUND.` · `ONE FAITH, LOCAL CUSTOMS.` · then, large: `LET EVERY MAN ABOUND IN HIS OWN SENSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a custom unlike yours. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a way of praying, or a habit at church, that isn't yours. A veil, a raised hand, a silence that felt too long, a song that felt too loud. Picture one real person who keeps it. Ask what it might hold for them: a memory, a family, a way of saying yes to God. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. If you don't, simply wish them well in the thing they love. The bell holds the time.
Many customs. The Catholic understanding that one faith and one Mass can be kept with different local habits: veils, postures, music and silence. Today's word.
Your line: many customs. Today, when someone does a familiar thing differently, the dishes, a holiday, a prayer, ask about it before you correct it. Day one thousand four hundred three.

howItsDone: Catholic customs at Mass vary by country and parish: some women wear a chapel veil and others don't, bishops' conferences adapt when the people kneel or stand, and parishes differ in music, language and silence. Visitors are generally expected to follow the custom of the parish they're in.

fork.setup: you're Monica. you've moved to Milan, and the church here doesn't fast on Saturday the way your home church did. what do you do?
options: keep your old fast, so no one thinks you've gone soft.
have your son ask the bishop, Ambrose, what to do.
stop going to church until you find one that does it your way.
fork.reveal: Augustine asked Ambrose for her. the bishop said he fasted on Saturday in Rome and not in Milan: follow the church you're in. Augustine says he took it as if from heaven.

original.note: Latin, custom: the word Church law uses for a long-kept local practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: one parish does it right and the other does it wrong.
what it means: one faith and one Mass, kept with different local habits of posture, music, dress and silence.

what a scholar hears: Augustine's letter recording Ambrose's rule on the Saturday fast, and the Second Vatican Council's line that the Church doesn't want rigid uniformity where the faith isn't at stake.

sources.quoted: One judgeth between day and day: and another judgeth every day: let every man abound in his own sense.

sources.ref: Augustine, Letter 54 (to Januarius), on the Saturday fast and Ambrose's answer
General Instruction of the Roman Missal 43

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Romans 14:5: confirm exactly ('For one judgeth...' — the leading 'For' is dropped in the quotation).

Augustine's account of Monica, Ambrose and the Saturday fast: paraphrased from Letter 54 (to Januarius); a related account is in Letter 36. Confirm the letter number and that Augustine says he received the answer 'as if from heaven'.
Sacrosanctum Concilium 37 (no rigid uniformity in matters not implicating the faith or the good of the whole community): paraphrased; confirm.
GIRM 43: postures may be adapted by the conference of bishops. Paraphrased; confirm.
Veils described only as 'worn by choice' with no claim about canon law history; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with that framing.
Original: 'consuetudo' as Church law's word for custom (Code of Canon Law, canons 23–28); confirm pronunciation.
